newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia fears consequences of American's murder.
newsitem.headline: Russia fears consequences of American's murder.

text.p: Friends of murdered American businessman Paul Tatum said on Tuesday that his death threatened Russia's relations with the West, but Moscow's foreign ministry said it hoped it would not upset ties with Washington.

An eclectic gathering from the Russian arts world and the Orthodox church joined forces at a news conference to demand a full investigation of the case and praise Tatum, who they said had been unjustly labelled an "adventurer" in the Russian media.

Organisers said U.S. colleagues of Tatum had been due to come but were advised to keep away for their own safety by the U.S. embassy. Tatum, 41, was gunned down on November 3 in the street outside a hotel whose ownership he was disputing.
The embassy, which last week said it deplored the murder, was not immediately available for comment.

Tatum's murder is just one of a spate of contract killings of businessmen in Russia but it was the first time an American had been targeted, sending shivers through Moscow's already jittery foreign business community.

Fears that the criminal underworld which has grown up in the aftermath of the collapse of communism has got beyond the reach of the authorities increased on Sunday with the brutal murder of more than a dozen mourners in a Moscow cemetery.

Human remains were blown all over the area by a bomb placed near the grave in what investigators said was the latest stage in a longstanding feud between crime groups linked to charities set up to help Afghan war veterans.

Itar-Tass news agency said on Tuesday a new victim had been identified from body parts, taking the death toll to 14. Thirteen people were in hospital, 10 of them seriously injured, including a 10-year-old boy who had to have an eye removed.

Three of Tatum's Russian friends -- an academic, a journalist and a writer -- distributed a statement in which they said his murder stood out from the stream of similar killings because it involved a foreigner.

"A blow has been struck against the very possibility of Russia's convergence with the western world, not only because it casts doubt over Russia's ability to reform and blocks western credits but because it is above all a crime against a human being," the statement said.
They said Tatum, from Oklahoma, had contributed to the Russian Orthodox church, charities and the arts, including the cash-strapped Bolshoi Theatre. He was to be buried on Thursday.

They said he was naive but far from the trouble-seeker he was portrayed in some media accounts of his row with his Russian partners in the Radisson-Slavyanskaya hotel, one of the first Russian-U.S. joint ventures and the favoured Moscow residence of visiting U.S. officials, including President Bill Clinton.

"We, friends and colleagues of Paul Tatum, will not give up haunting the threshold of the security forces with futile demands for this act of terrorism to be uncovered more quickly," said the statement.
Contract killings are on the increase in Russia's chaotic and crime-ridden post-communist economy and police admit they have made little progress in resolving even high profile cases.
But foreign ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin said on Tuesday the interior ministry and security police were both investigating the Tatum case, which he hoped would be resolved quickly.
"The necessary investigative activities are being vigorously conducted," Demurin told a news briefing.
"We would like to hope...that this tragic happening will not affect the development of trade and economic relations between our countries," he said.
